subject: physics
question_text: Derive an expression for the work done by a variable force.

verification.note: PREDICTED — Session 89 enumeration sweep (archetype × object grid over the NCERT chapter): this question has not appeared in any paper or source book we hold, but the chapter contains it and the 2-mark/4-mark format admits it. Authored as a lean card; promote to a full card when a paper season or a Telangana IPE teacher validates the cell. Split invented, as everywhere.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The difficulty
lines: For a constant force, W = F S cos θ. A
variable force has a different value at every
point of the path, so no single F can be put
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say why W = F S cos θ cannot be used here. That sentence is the mark.
steps.why: Naming why the constant-force formula fails is what earns the first mark; the rest of the answer is the repair.
common_mistakes: Using the average of the first and last values of F, which is only correct for a force that grows linearly.

recall.must_convey: That a variable force has a different value at every point, so the constant force formula cannot be used directly.
accept: the constant force formula does not apply
reject: split the path into small displacements

steps.memory_tip: A spring is the standard example: F = kx is different at every point of the stretch.

steps.label: Splitting the path
lines: Split the path into displacements Δx so small
that F is practically constant over each one.
Over one such piece the work is
Adding the pieces over the whole path,
steps.margin_note: Two marks. One for the small piece ΔW = F(x)Δx, one for the sum over the whole path.
steps.why: Every hard quantity in physics is handled this way: cut the change into pieces small enough for the easy formula to hold, then add them up.
common_mistakes: Taking Δx large, so that F is not constant over the piece and the step is not valid.

recall.must_convey: That the path is split into small displacements over which F is nearly constant, and the small works are added.
accept: F is nearly constant over each piece

steps.memory_tip: Thin rectangles under a curve: each one is F(x)Δx, and the sum of them is the work.

steps.label: The result
lines: As Δx is made smaller and smaller, the sum
becomes the area under the curve:

lines.text: W = area under the F – x graph

lines: Area below the axis counts as negative work.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Box the area statement, then add the line about area below the axis.
steps.why: The graph reading is what an examiner tests, and it makes the sign of the work visible without any algebra.
common_mistakes: Ignoring the sign of the area, so that a retarding force adds instead of subtracting.

recall.must_convey: That the work done equals the area under the force displacement graph.
accept: area under the F x graph
area under the force displacement curve

steps.memory_tip: Spring: the F–x line is straight, so the area is the triangle ½kx². The same answer.

insider_note: Splitting the path carries 2 of the 4 marks. Write ΔW = F(x)Δx and the sum; the graph area alone is only the last mark.
